notes.text: Thirsteth — For the grace of God and the blessings of the gospel. This thirst implies a vehement, and active, and restless desire after it. No money - Those who are most worthless and wicked, if they do but thirst may be welcome. Buy - Procure or receive that which is freely offered. Wine and milk - All gospel-blessings; in particular, that peace and joy in the Holy Ghost, which are better than wine, and that love of God which nourishes the soul, as milk does the body.

Money — All your time, and strength, and cost. Not bread - For those things which can never nourish or satisfy you, such as worldly goods, or pleasures. Eat ye - That which is truly and solidly, and everlastingly good. In fatness - In this pleasant food of gospel-enjoyments.

An everlasting covenant — That everlasting covenant of grace and peace which I made with Abraham, and his seed. Of David - Even that covenant which was made first with Abraham, and then with David, concerning those glorious and sure blessings which God hath promised to his people, one and the chief of which was giving Christ to die for their sins. David here seems to be put for the son of David.

Behold — I have appointed, and will in due time actually give. Him - The David last mentioned, even Christ. A witness - To declare the will of God concerning the duty and salvation of men, to bear witness to truth, to confirm God's promises, and, among others, those which respect the calling of the Gentiles: to be a witness of both parties of that covenant made between God and men. The people - To all people.

Thou — Thou, O Messiah. Call - To the knowledge of thyself. Knewest not - With that special knowledge which implies approbation. Because - Because the Lord shall by many tokens, manifest himself to be thy God, and thee to be his son and faithful servant. Glorify thee - By confirming thy word with illustrious signs and miracles, and particularly by thy resurrection, and glorious ascension.

Seek — labour to get the knowledge of God's will, and to obtain his grace and favour. While - In this day of grace, while he offers mercy and reconciliation. Near - Ready and desirous to receive you to mercy.
Return — By sincere repentance, and faith.

For — If any man injure you, especially if he do it greatly and frequently, you are slow and backward to forgive him. But I am ready to forgive all penitents, how many, and great, and numberless soever their sins be.

glossa.text:
*All you that thirst, come.* ((HIER.)) Because he had said that the vessel fashioned against the Church was to be broken, and every tongue armed against the knowledge of God to be overcome, he calls believers to the river of God, which is filled with waters.

*Eat ye.* By hearing, by speaking, by reading, by meditating, by working, by keeping in the heart. For the divine Scripture is both drink, when open, and food, when hidden. It is also both the water and the bread that came down from heaven.

*Why do you weigh out silver.* You weigh the sacred words, but not the refreshment. You who keep the appearance of the letter alone lose, from the spiritual understanding, the fatness of the inward refreshment.

*Behold, a witness.* He challenged the Jews to believe, but because he knew that, when they did not believe, the Gentiles were going to believe, he says that he has sent his Son to announce his precepts to the peoples.
*The Lord thy God.* ((ID.)) When he is called Father, the Father of Christ is called, according to the divinity, the Father of glory; according to the humanity, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

*Seek ye the Lord.* These things pertain to the Jews or to the Gentiles specially, and to each one generally. The prophet to the Jews: *Seek ye the Lord,* as though he said: The Gentiles receive the mercies of David, and you disdain them; but do penance, and be converted while you have time.

 *Whilst he is near.* ((ID.)) Lest by your vices he withdraw, who draws near to those who draw near to him, and runs to meet the returning son with gladness.
*For not.* Do not think that what I promise is hard: consider that between my counsels and yours there is much difference: and as great as is the diversity of nature, so great is that of will.

notes.text: Early — Hebrew. in the morning, Which implies the doing it with diligence and speed. Thirsteth - For the enjoyment of thee in thy house and ordinances. Flesh - The desire of my soul, is so vehement, that my very body feels the effects of it. No water - In a land where I want the refreshing waters of the sanctuary.
To see — To enjoy. Power - The powerful and glorious effects of thy gracious presence.
Satisfied — When thou shalt fulfil my earnest desire of enjoying thee in the sanctuary.

glossa.text: *O God, my God, to thee from the light,* etc. ((Ibid.)) How she fares in the desert, namely the bride, she desires to see God, whom she also praises, and she wishes to do this the more. *God. ((Ibid.))* Common, *my God* in a somewhat more particular way; see the affection of devout entreaty through this doubling. *From the light.* Or at daybreak, when Christ rose again, that the Church may praise him then, when by the example of his own resurrection he quickened her to rise. *I watch,* even while I sleep, not loving the things that are of the world. ((CASS.)) And I thirst in mind and in body. *From the light.* ((AUG.)) For thou wouldst not watch; unless the light arose, which should rouse thee. *My soul hath thirsted for thee:* and here the flesh for God, while it seeks from him the things needful here.

*Desert. ((Ibid.))* Where none of the saints dwells. *Trackless,* because there is no way by which thou mayest go out thence. *Waterless,* because neither, while thou tarriest where thou art, is there water there. But God here made a way, Christ, and sent the water of his Word, filling the preachers with the Holy Ghost: *That there might be made in them a fountain of water springing up into life everlasting ((Joan. IV))*. *So in the sanctuary have I appeared to thee, that I might see,* etc. ((AUG.)) He to whom God does not appear, let him be in holy desire, etc., *as far as* For the sun by its own light makes us to see, and so also does God.

*Above lives. ((Ibid.))* Of human life, of which there are many, as that of the soldier, of the husbandman and of the rest: better is what thou givest to the corrected than what the perverse choose. *My lips.* After the benefits of God: he promises praise. *Shall praise,* toward my neighbour, for whom also I am solicitous, because unless thy mercy went before me, I could not praise thee, and as with the lips, so let them bless in life. Or thus, *Because above lives.*

*Thus will I bless. ((Ibid.))* As thou hast granted, through mercy, that I should praise thee, *so will I bless,* that I may ascribe to mercy the life in which I praise. *In thy name I will lift up my hands. ((Ibid.))* He lifts up his hands who, persevering in good works, with hands stretched out in the figure of the cross, adores God unde; whence the Apostle: Lifting up pure hands in prayer, without anger and contention.

*With fatness. ((Ibid.))* In the inward parts. Fatness is in the flesh, that is, wisdom, which is in secret, and the strength of the spirit.

*I will lift up my hands. ((Ibid.))* In Exodus. Moses, while he lifted up his hands to the Lord, etc., *as far as* he works for earthly things, he is overcome by Amalec.

*If I have remembered.* ((CASS.)) He sets forth the good things and the evil of either party, etc., *as far as* save he who works in Christ.

((CASS.)) *In the mornings,* that is, in the light of Christ, as above, *from the light I watch unto thee,* that the son of light, that is, of Christ, may watch unto the author of light, unto God.
*A helper,* etc. ((AUG.)) In the perils of Idumaea, etc., *atc.* *as far as* because *it hath upheld me* from perils, *thy right hand,* that is, propitiation.

notes.text: Now — That ye may not become reprobates, consider how highly favoured your fathers were, who were God's elect and peculiar people, and nevertheless were rejected by him. They were all under the cloud - That eminent token of God's gracious presence, which screened them from the heat of the sun by day, and gave them light by night. And all passed through the sea - God opening a way through the midst of the waters. Exod. xiii, 21 Exod. xiv, 22

And were all, as it were, baptized unto Moses — initiated into the religion which he taught them. In the cloud and in the sea - Perhaps sprinkled here and there with drops of water from the sea or the cloud, by which baptism might be the more evidently signified.

And all ate the same manna, termed spiritual meat, as it was typical,

1. Of Christ and his spiritual benefits:

2. Of the sacred bread which we eat at his table. Exod. xvi, 15.

And all drank the same spiritual drink — Typical of Christ, and of that cup which we drink. For they drank out of the spiritual or mysterious rock, the wonderful streams of which followed them in their several journeyings, for many years, through the wilderness. And that rock was a manifest type of Christ - The Rock of Eternity, from whom his people derive those streams of blessings which follow them through all this wilderness. Exod. xvii, 6.
Yet — Although they had so many tokens of the divine presence. They were overthrown - With the most terrible marks of his displeasure.

Now these things were our examples — Showing what we are to expect if, enjoying the like benefits, we commit the like sins. The benefits are set down in the same order as by Moses in Exodus; the sins and punishments in a different order; evil desire first, as being the foundation of all; next, idolatry, ver. 7, 14; then fornication, which usually accompanied it, ver. 8; the tempting and murmuring against God, in the following verses. As they desired - Flesh, in contempt of manna. Num. xi, 4

Neither be ye idolaters — And so, "neither murmur ye," ver. 10. The other cautions are given in the first person; but these in the second. And with what exquisite propriety does he vary the person! It would have been improper to say, Neither let us be idolaters; for he was himself in no danger of idolatry; nor probably of murmuring against Christ, or the divine providence. To play - That is, to dance, in honour of their idol. Exod. xxxii, 6.
And fell in one day three and twenty thousand — Beside the princes who were afterwards hanged, and those whom the Judges slew so that there died in all four and twenty thousand. Num. xxv, 1, 9.

Neither let us tempt Christ — By our unbelief. St. Paul enumerates five benefits, ver. 1-4; of which the fourth and fifth were closely connected together; and five sins, the fourth and fifth of which were likewise closely connected. In speaking of the fifth benefit, he expressly mentions Christ; and in speaking of the fourth sin, he shows it was committed against Christ. As some of them tempted him - This sin of the people was peculiarly against Christ; for when they had so long drank of that rock, yet they murmured for want of water. Num. xxi, 4, &c.
The destroyer — The destroying angel. Num. xiv, 1, 36

On whom the ends of the ages are come — The expression has great force. All things meet together, and come to a crisis, under the last, the gospel, dispensation; both benefits and dangers, punishments and rewards. It remains, that Christ come as an avenger and judge. And even these ends include various periods, succeeding each other.
The common translation runs, Let him that thinketh he standeth; but the word translated thinketh, most certainly strengthens, rather than weakens, the sense.

Common to man — Or, as the Greek word imports, proportioned to human strength. God is faithful - In giving the help which he hath promised. And he will with the temptation - Provide for your deliverance.

glossa.text: *For I would not.* He who wishes to lay hold must so act; for baptism and the sacraments do not suffice, as some think; even as neither did the benefits of God avail the Jews, since they afterwards sinned. *That our fathers.* By the example of the Jews, who by their own negligence gave offence, he makes them anxious. *Under the cloud.* Because all things befell them in a figure of us.

*Baptized in Moses.* Under the leadership of Moses, purged through those signs that were seen. Or, they received the sign of baptism, which availed the same for believers. *They were baptized,* because they were freed from death and through it cleansed from the ignorance of God which pressed upon all the nations, and made ready for receiving the law. Or they are said to be baptized because they bore the form of our sacrament. Moses signifies Christ, the cloud the Holy Spirit, the sea baptism.

*The same meat.* That is, in faith: diverse in time, diverse in appearance. *Spiritual.* That is, signifying something spiritual. When he says *spiritual,* he shows that it is to be understood spiritually in Christ, and this he intimates of them all, and expounds one: *The rock was Christ.*

*The rock following them.* That is, satisfying their will, because wheresoever they went, overflowing waters followed; so Christ accompanies his own in the desert of this world. Or, *following,* that is, signifying the truth that was to follow after. *And the rock.* A thing which is signified is wont to be named by the name of the thing which it signifies. *The rock.* That is, Christ, was following, because where human support failed, he was at hand.

*Neither become idolaters,* etc. He touches those who feasted in the idol's temple, thinking themselves free from crime. *The people sat down.* By the commemoration of those things he marks what things are in the Corinthians, showing how gravely they were punished in the Jews. *To play.* That is, to adore, which is like the play of boys. For childhood is prone to play. And what is so like to a boyish game as to adore idols?

*Neither let us tempt Christ.* Note Christ as God, whom the Jews tempted, and therefore they perished by serpents, until the brazen serpent was raised up, and they who looked upon it were healed of the bites.
*In a figure.* Behold, he shows why those signs are no longer observed, since the thing is made manifest for our correction.

*They are written.* Not for us only. For by these examples we are stirred up to a more corrected life, that we may merit either a reward, if we have been obedient, or a heavier punishment if disobedient. *The ends of the world.* Because we are in the last age, and by so many examples of those before us we ought the more to be corrected. Or the ends of the world have come upon us, worldliness is ended in us; and therefore it is the more shameful if we sin.

*Let him take heed lest he fall.* As those who, presuming upon knowledge, ate things offered to idols with scandal to the brethren, and glorying in the false ones, judged the apostle, whereas they themselves were guilty.

*Let no temptation take hold of you,* etc. He exhorts that human temptation may take hold of them, not another. For human temptation is this, that in necessity or in pressure a man should not distrust God, by seeking human help. Therefore to suffer for Christ is a human temptation, whereby profit is made with God.

*That you may be able to bear it.* Which is done through humility. For he keeps the humble in every temptation, so that they do not burst in the furnace who have not the wind of pride.

notes.text: The Galileans, whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices — Some of the followers of Judas Gaulonites. They absolutely refused to own the Roman authority. Pilate surrounded and slew them, while they were worshipping in the temple, at a public feast.

Ye shall all likewise perish — All ye of Galilee and of Jerusalem shall perish in the very same manner. So the Greek word implies. And so they did. There was a remarkable resemblance between the fate of these Galileans and of the main body of the Jewish nation; the flower of which was slain at Jerusalem by the Roman sword, while they were assembled at one of their great festivals. And many thousands of them perished in the temple itself, and were literally buried under its ruins.

A man had a fig tree — Either we may understand God the Father by him that had the vineyard, and Christ by him that kept it: or Christ himself is he that hath it, and his ministers they that keep it. Psalm lxxx, 8. &c.

Three years — Christ was then in the third year of his ministry. But it may mean only several years; a certain number being put for an uncertain. Why doth it also cumber the ground? - That is, not only bear no fruit itself, but take up the ground of another tree that would.

glossa.text: *And there were present.* While the master of truth was instructing those present how they ought to prepare themselves for the coming of the judge, and how they that do not prepare themselves are to be condemned, tidings are brought him of the Galileans, who as it were justly sought this for the cause that they had not well prepared themselves: and the Lord answers both that they truly had been sinners and had justly perished, and that other sinners shall likewise perish, if they take no heed that they are sinners. *Bringing tidings.* As if they said: It appears that these men were sinners and to be condemned for ever, who by so wicked a death were slain by an impious governor in the midst of their own sacrifices. *Of the Galileans.* The Galileans pay the impious penalties of their own crimes by a wicked death; yet it was not that death itself that harmed them, so that they should be sent into the second death, but their wicked life. And they were punished for the correction of the living, that when the pestilent man is scourged the fool may become wiser, or for an example to those who will not be corrected, and who therefore shall perish most wretchedly.

*All,* etc. This was fulfilled after the Lord's passion, when the Romans so laid waste the impenitent Jews, beginning from Galilee, that not only the courts of the temple but even the inner parts of the house, whither the Galileans had no access, were defiled with human blood.

*As those eighteen.* These men of Jerusalem, like the Galileans also, were not the only sinners, but were punished for the terror of the rest; and they, crushed by the fall of the tower, signify that the Jews who would not repent were to perish together with their own walls. Nor is it without purpose that they are eighteen, which number among the Greeks is expressed by iota and ita, that is, by the same letters with which the name Jesus begins. And it signifies that those Jews chiefly were to perish who would not receive the name of the Saviour. That tower signifies him who is the tower of strength, which is rightly in Siloe, because Siloe, which is interpreted *sent,* signifies him who, sent by the Father, came into the world, who shall crush all upon whom he shall fall.

*A fig tree.* In the beginning of the human race Adam and Eve, when they had sinned, made themselves aprons of fig leaves. By the leaves of the fig tree, therefore, sins are understood. And they were under the fig tree as under the shadow of death, of whom it is said: *They that sat under the shadow of death, light is risen to them ((Isa. XI))*.

*Seeking fruit. The vineyard of the Lord sabaoh is the house of Israel,* in which house the Synagogue was founded as a fig tree in a vineyard. But he who permitted the one sinning in the vineyard to be plundered by wayfarers commanded this fig tree also to be cut down. In it he seeks fruit, not as one who did not know that it was there, but he shows in a figure that in the Synagogue it ought by now to have fruit. Nor does he seek before the time, who comes through three years. He who through Moses established the Synagogue, himself appearing in the flesh teaches often in the Synagogue, seeks the fruit of faith, but finds it not in the Pharisees.

*And he said to the dresser of the vineyard.* The dresser of the vineyard: these are the teachers and the apostles, by whose prayers and admonitions the unceasing care of God is supplied; to whom the Lord often complains of the unfruitful nation of the Jews, that through the three years of his visitation, that is, in the edicts of the law, in the testimonies of the prophets, in the grace of the Gospel, it has been negligent.

*Why doth it also the ground,* etc. By the ground occupied by the barren fig tree may be signified the Jewish people, which is pressed by the harmful shadow of its rulers, that it may not see the light of truth, and is hindered by their examples, that it may not grow warm with the sun of love; whence ((Matth. XXIII)): *Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees,* etc. He occupies the ground who does not work with good works the place that he holds, who by the example of his crookedness affords a hindrance to the rest.

*Until I dig,* etc. That is, until I make the root of the unfruitful mind humble, by striking into it the fear both of present afflictions and of eternal damnation. For a ditch is in the lowest place, and rebuke, while it shows the mind to itself, humbles it. He knows how to till the ground who knows how to reprove vices. He understood that the hardness and pride of the Jews was the cause of their barrenness. And so he promises that hard hearts are to be dug with apostolic mattocks, and proud hearts to be called back to humility. *And put on dung.* That is, I will bring back to their mind the abomination of the evils they have done, and will rouse up the grace of compunction, with the fruits of good work, as it were from the richness of the dung. For the sins of the flesh are called dung, which are laid to the root of the tree when the memory of the thought touches the conscience of its own crookedness; and while a man repents thereof, he returns, as it were by the touch of dung, to the fruitfulness of work.

*And if indeed.* Although the order of repentance required that he should add "it shall be spared," or something of the kind, yet he subjoined nothing, but left the sentence hanging.

*But if not.* That is, if it shall not bear fruit, he at once annexed the judgment of the damnation to come, because he saw men more prone to deny than to believe.

echoes.text: Yahweh went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, to lead them on their way, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light, that they might go by day and by night: the pillar of cloud by day, and the pillar of fire by night, didn’t depart from before the people.
echoes.note: The pillar of cloud leading Israel is the referent of 'our fathers were all under the cloud.' High volume and availability; Paul reads the wilderness narrative typologically, making the cloud a figure of the divine covering shared by all. Coherence with the baptismal reading of v.2 confirms the allusion.

echoes.text: The angel of God, who went before the camp of Israel, moved and went behind them; and the pillar of cloud moved from before them, and stood behind them. It came between the camp of Egypt and the camp of Israel; and there was the cloud and the darkness, yet gave it light by night: and the one didn’t come near the other all the night.
echoes.note: The angel-and-cloud standing between Egypt and Israel at the sea supplies the dual cloud/sea imagery Paul fuses in vv.1-2. Recurrence of the cloud motif and its narrative pairing with the sea-crossing make this a strong contributor to 'under the cloud.'

echoes.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all the night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. The children of Israel went into the midst of the sea on the dry ground, and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand, and on their left.
echoes.note: 'All passed through the sea' directly invokes the Red Sea crossing on dry ground between walls of water. High volume and availability; Paul makes the crossing a type of baptism (v.2), the controlling figural reading of the pericope.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not. It shall come to pass on the sixth day, that they shall prepare that which they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they gather daily.” Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel, “At evening, then you shall know that Yahweh has brought […]
echoes.note: The manna is the 'spiritual food' all ate. The chapter's wilderness frame and Paul's emphasis on 'the same' food for all point to the daily bread from heaven. He reads it figurally as sacramental nourishment prefiguring Christ.

echoes.text: Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock in Horeb. You shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it, that the people may drink.” Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel.
echoes.note: Water struck from the rock at Horeb is the 'spiritual drink.' High volume; combined with Numbers 20 it grounds 'the Rock was Christ.' Paul's figural identification of the rock with Christ depends on these water-from-rock episodes.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Take the rod, and assemble the congregation, you, and Aaron your brother, and speak to the rock before their eyes, that it pour out its water. You shall bring water to them out of the rock; so you shall give the congregation and their livestock drink.” Moses took the rod from before Yahweh, as he commanded him. Moses and Aaron gathered the assembly together before the rock, and he said to them, “Hear now, you rebels! Shall […]
echoes.note: The second water-from-rock event at Meribah supplies the geographic span (beginning and end of the wilderness) that fuels the haggadic 'rock that followed them.' Recurrence of two rock-events at opposite ends of the journey underlies the moving-rock tradition Paul presupposes.

echoes.text: Your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness; and all who were numbered of you, according to your whole number, from twenty years old and upward, who have murmured against me, surely you shall not come into the land, concerning which I swore that I would make you dwell therein, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua the son of Nun.
echoes.note: 'Your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness' is the source of 'they were overthrown in the wilderness' (v.5). High volume and verbal coherence with kateströthēsan; the wilderness-generation's exclusion is Paul's typological warning to the Corinthians.

echoes.text: On the day that the tabernacle was raised up, the cloud covered the tabernacle, even the Tent of the Testimony: and at evening it was over the tabernacle as it were the appearance of fire, until morning. So it was continually. The cloud covered it, and the appearance of fire by night. Whenever the cloud was taken up from over the Tent, then after that the children of Israel traveled; and in the place where the cloud remained, there the children of Israel […]
echoes.note: The cloud covering the tabernacle and regulating Israel's movements reinforces the 'under the cloud' language as a sustained guiding-presence motif, not a single event. Lower volume than Exodus 13 but adds recurrence to the cloud tradition Paul draws on.

echoes.text: He spread a cloud for a covering, fire to give light in the night.
echoes.note: 'He spread a cloud for a covering' summarizes the Exodus cloud in a single liturgical line that may stand closer to Paul's compressed phrasing than the narrative itself. The psalm's recital of wilderness mercies (cloud, sea, manna, water from the rock) parallels Paul's own catalogue, suggesting a psalmic mediation of the tradition.

echoes.text: He rained down manna on them to eat, and gave them food from the sky. Man ate the bread of angels. He sent them food to the full.
echoes.note: 'He rained down manna... grain of heaven... bread of the mighty' interprets the manna as heavenly bread, close to Paul's 'spiritual food.' The psalm's theological reading of the wilderness gifts coheres with Paul's, making it a plausible mediating source alongside Exodus 16.

echoes.text: He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth.
echoes.note: 'Man does not live by bread alone... but by every word' interprets the manna as more than physical sustenance, supporting Paul's 'spiritual' qualifier. Moderate volume; the Deuteronomic theology of manna as God-given instruction coheres with Paul's sacramental reading.

echoes.text: He split rocks in the wilderness, and gave them drink abundantly as out of the depths. He brought streams also out of the rock, and caused waters to run down like rivers.
echoes.note: 'He split rocks... brought streams... waters run down like rivers' poeticizes the water-from-rock miracle and may inform 'drank of a spiritual rock.' The psalm's abundance language coheres with Paul's claim that all drank the same drink.

echoes.text: He opened the rock, and waters gushed out. They ran as a river in the dry places.
echoes.note: 'He opened the rock, and water gushed out; it flowed through the desert like a river' depicts water following Israel through the wilderness, the nearest scriptural seed of the 'rock that followed them.' Strong coherence with the moving-water tradition Paul assumes.

echoes.text: The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are just. A God of faithfulness who does no wrong, just and right is he.
echoes.note: 'The Rock, his work is perfect' establishes the Song of Moses' titular use of 'the Rock' (haTsur) for God, the theological backbone of 'the Rock was Christ.' Paul's identification trades on this divine-Rock title, not merely the water episodes.

echoes.text: But Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked. You have grown fat. You have grown thick. You have become sleek. Then he abandoned God who made him, and rejected the Rock of his salvation.
echoes.note: 'Forsook God... scoffed at the Rock of his salvation' continues the Song's Rock-title for God amid the very apostasy Paul is warning against. Recurrence within the Song he draws on elsewhere in the chapter (vv.17,21) strengthens the link.

echoes.text: ‘Because Yahweh was not able to bring this people into the land which he swore to them, therefore he has slain them in the wilderness.’
echoes.note: 'The LORD was not able to bring this people in... he slaughtered them in the wilderness' supplies the 'God was not well pleased' / 'overthrown' theme. Coherence with v.5's divine displeasure motif.

echoes.text: when the anger of God went up against them, killed some of their fattest, and struck down the young men of Israel.
echoes.note: 'The anger of God came up against them... and struck down... the young men of Israel' poeticizes the wilderness destruction Paul invokes in v.5. The psalm's wilderness-judgment recital parallels Paul's whole catalogue.

echoes.text: Forty long years I was grieved with that generation, and said, “It is a people that errs in their heart. They have not known my ways.” Therefore I swore in my wrath, “They won’t enter into my rest.”
echoes.note: 'Forty years... they shall not enter my rest' expresses God's displeasure with the wilderness generation, matching 'God was not well pleased.' A liturgical summary of the very judgment Paul applies typologically.

echoes.text: Of the Rock who became your father, you are unmindful, and have forgotten God who gave you birth.
echoes.note: 'You forgot the Rock that bore you' adds the begetting-Rock image to the divine-Rock cluster. Low volume on its own, but it belongs to the Song of Moses substratum that pervades 1 Cor 10's rock and demon language.

echoes.text: How could one chase a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, unless their Rock had sold them, and Yahweh had delivered them up? For their rock is not as our Rock, even our enemies themselves concede.
echoes.note: 'Their Rock had sold them... their rock is not as our Rock' juxtaposes Israel's God-Rock against the enemies' rock, sharpening the Rock title. Faint here but coheres with Paul's polemical use of Deut 32 across the chapter.

echoes.text: They rose up early on the next day, and offered burnt offerings, and brought peace offerings; and the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play.
echoes.note: 'The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play' is quoted verbatim (v.7) from the golden-calf episode, marked 'as it is written.' Highest volume; the calf is Paul's paradigm of idolatry feasting, directly relevant to the idol-meat question.

echoes.text: When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down from the mountain, the people gathered themselves together to Aaron, and said to him, “Come, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we don’t know what has become of him.” Aaron said to them, “Take off the golden rings, which are in the ears of your wives, of your sons, and of your daughters, and bring them to me.” All the people […]
echoes.note: The golden-calf narrative as a whole supplies 'neither be idolaters, as some of them were' (v.7). The calf is the controlling type of idolatrous communal feasting that frames Paul's argument about meals offered to idols.

echoes.text: Israel stayed in Shittim; and the people began to play the prostitute with the daughters of Moab; for they called the people to the sacrifices of their gods. The people ate and bowed down to their gods. Israel joined himself to Baal Peor. Yahweh’s anger was kindled against Israel. Yahweh said to Moses, “Take all the chiefs of the people, and hang them up to Yahweh before the sun, that the fierce anger of Yahweh may turn away from Israel.” Moses said to […]
echoes.note: The Baal-Peor apostasy, where Israel committed sexual immorality with Moabite women and a plague killed many, is the type behind v.8. High volume and coherence; Paul's 23,000 reworks the Numbers death toll for his warning against porneia.

echoes.text: The people spoke against God, and against Moses, “Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is no bread, and there is no water; and our soul loathes this light bread.” Yahweh sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people. Many people of Israel died.
echoes.note: The fiery serpents sent because the people spoke against God supply 'perished by the serpents' (v.9). High volume; the serpent plague is the type for testing God/Christ, directly named by Paul.

echoes.text: But on the next day all the congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron, saying, “You have killed Yahweh’s people!” When the congregation was assembled against Moses and against Aaron, They looked toward the Tent of Meeting. Behold, the cloud covered it, and Yahweh’s glory appeared. Moses and Aaron came to the front of the Tent of Meeting. Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Get away from among this congregation, that I may […]
echoes.note: After Korah, the congregation grumbled against Moses and Aaron and a plague (stopped by the destroyer/atonement) killed 14,700, the type behind 'neither grumble... perished by the destroyer' (v.10). High coherence between the grumbling-then-plague pattern and Paul's clause.

echoes.text: The mixed multitude that was among them lusted exceedingly: and the children of Israel also wept again, and said, “Who will give us flesh to eat?
echoes.note: 'The rabble had a strong craving... who will give us meat to eat?' grounds 'we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted' (v.6). The verb epethymēsan echoes the craving narrative; coherence with the wilderness-craving judgment.

echoes.text: The name of that place was called Kibroth Hattaavah, because there they buried the people who lusted.
echoes.note: Kibroth-hattaavah, 'the graves of craving,' names the place where the people who lusted were buried, the etiological seed of Paul's 'lust after evil things.' High coherence with v.6's craving-and-death pattern.

echoes.text: but gave in to craving in the desert, and tested God in the wasteland.
echoes.note: 'They lusted exceedingly in the wilderness, and tested God in the desert' compactly pairs lust and testing, both of which Paul enumerates (vv.6,9). The psalm's wilderness-sin catalogue is a likely template for Paul's list.

echoes.text: Those who died by the plague were twenty-four thousand.
echoes.note: Numbers reports 24,000 dead 'in one day'; Paul's 'twenty-three thousand fell in one day' alludes to this figure, the difference being a known harmonization crux. The 'in one day' phrase strengthens the verbal tie even as the number varies.

echoes.text: All the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron. The whole congregation said to them, “We wish that we had died in the land of Egypt, or that we had died in this wilderness!
echoes.note: 'All the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron' supplies the murmuring motif that ends in wilderness death. Plausible alongside Num 16 as the referent for 'as some of them also grumbled.'

echoes.text: For Yahweh will pass through to strike the Egyptians; and when he sees the blood on the lintel, and on the two door posts, Yahweh will pass over the door, and will not allow the destroyer to come in to your houses to strike you.
echoes.note: 'The LORD will not allow the destroyer to enter' names ha-mashchit, 'the destroyer,' the agent Paul invokes in v.10. The Passover destroyer is reapplied to the wilderness-grumbling judgment, supplying Paul's exact figure.

echoes.text: They tempted God in their heart by asking food according to their desire.
echoes.note: 'They tested God in their heart by asking food' offers the 'test' vocabulary Paul uses in v.9. Faint, but coheres with the psalmic wilderness-testing tradition behind his catalogue.

echoes.text: even those men who brought up an evil report of the land, died by the plague before Yahweh.
echoes.note: The death of the faithless spies 'by a plague before the LORD' caps the wilderness judgments Paul says 'happened to them by way of example' (v.11). Faint summary tie reinforcing the typological frame, not a specific verbal echo.

echoes.text: You shall remember all the way which Yahweh your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to prove you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments, or not.
echoes.note: 'Remember the whole way the LORD led you... to test you' frames the wilderness as instructive testing, coherent with 'written for our admonition' and the temptation theme of v.13. Low volume; offered for the didactic-wilderness coherence.

echoes.text: Know therefore that Yahweh your God himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with them who love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations,
echoes.note: 'Know that the LORD your God is the faithful God' underlies 'God is faithful' (v.13). The covenant-faithfulness predicate is a Deuteronomic commonplace Paul likely draws on for assurance amid testing.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Therefore I will judge you, house of Israel, everyone according to his ways, says the Lord Yahweh. Return, and turn yourselves from all your transgressions; so iniquity shall not be your ruin. Cast away from you all your transgressions, in which you have transgressed; and make yourself a new heart and a new spirit: for why will you die, house of Israel? For I have no pleasure in the death of him who dies, says the Lord Yahweh: therefore turn yourselves, […]
echoes.note: Jesus' refrain 'unless you repent, you will all perish' restates Ezekiel's prophetic logic that each person bears responsibility and must 'turn and live' lest he die. High Volume in the shared death/repentance vocabulary; strong Coherence with Luke's repentance theme; the prophet is widely available.

echoes.text: Tell them, As I live, says the Lord Yahweh, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn, turn from your evil ways; for why will you die, house of Israel?
echoes.note: 'I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that he turn from his way and live' supplies the same individualized call to repentance against assumed corporate judgment. Recurrence of Ezekiel's repent-or-perish motif strengthens the echo alongside 18:30-32.

echoes.text: “Remember, now, whoever perished, being innocent? Or where were the upright cut off?
echoes.note: Eliphaz's 'who ever perished, being innocent?' frames the retributive assumption ('worse sinners... because they suffered') that Jesus overturns. Faint and contested, but coherent with the OT debate over suffering as proof of guilt.

echoes.text: “Because this people have refused the waters of Shiloah that go softly, and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah’s son;
echoes.note: The 'waters of Shiloah' (Siloam) carry, in Isaiah, judgment imagery for those who reject the gentle stream; the tower 'in Siloam' may faintly evoke the site's prophetic charge. Low Volume and contested; geography may be incidental.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The owner of a vineyard who comes seeking fruit and finds none, threatening destruction, directly mirrors Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard, the canonical type for Israel's failure to yield justice. High Volume (vineyard + seeking fruit + judgment), strong Coherence, and prime Availability as the standard prophetic indictment.

echoes.text: I will utterly consume them, says Yahweh: no grapes shall be on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree, and the leaf shall fade; and the things that I have given them shall pass away from them.
echoes.note: 'There are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree' is Jeremiah's judgment oracle on fruitlessness, pairing the fig tree with the vineyard exactly as Luke does. Strong Volume in the fig-tree/no-fruit collocation and high Coherence with the threat to 'cut it down.'

echoes.text: Misery is mine! Indeed, I am like one who gathers the summer fruits, as gleanings of the vineyard: There is no cluster of grapes to eat. My soul desires to eat the early fig.
echoes.note: 'There is no cluster to eat; my soul desires the first-ripe fig' voices the same disappointed search for fruit on the fig tree as an image of a faithless people. Medium Volume; recurrence of the fruitless-fig motif across the prophets supports the echo.

echoes.text: I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness. I saw your fathers as the first ripe in the fig tree at its first season; but they came to Baal Peor, and consecrated themselves to the shameful thing, and became abominable like that which they loved.
echoes.note: Israel was found 'like the first fruit on the fig tree,' a hope reversed in 9:16 ('they shall bear no fruit'). The fig tree as figure for Israel's fruitfulness-turned-barren coheres tightly with the parable's verdict.

echoes.text: Ephraim is struck. Their root has dried up. They will bear no fruit. Even though they give birth, yet I will kill the beloved ones of their womb.”
echoes.note: 'Ephraim is struck down... they shall bear no fruit' supplies the barrenness-and-judgment outcome that the parable holds in suspense. Coherent with the prophetic fig-tree complex; medium Volume.

echoes.text: For though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines; the labor of the olive fails, the fields yield no food; the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls:
echoes.note: 'Though the fig tree does not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines' shares the fig-and-vine pairing for a season of barrenness. Faint here because Habakkuk's tone is trust amid loss rather than indictment; offered honestly as a low-confidence resonance.

echoes.text: He has laid my vine waste, and stripped my fig tree. He has stripped its bark, and thrown it away. Its branches are made white.
echoes.note: 'It has laid waste my vine and splintered my fig tree' joins vine and fig under devastation, the same agrarian pair behind Luke's parable. Low Volume and contested, but recurrence of the vine-fig motif gives it some weight.

echoes.text: You brought a vine out of Egypt. You drove out the nations, and planted it. You cleared the ground for it. It took deep root, and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shadow. Its boughs were like God’s cedars. It sent out its branches to the sea, Its shoots to the River. Why have you broken down its walls, so that all those who pass by the way pluck it? The boar out of the wood ravages it. The wild animals of the field feed on it. Turn […]
echoes.note: The vine brought out of Egypt, now burned and cut down for lack of protection, parallels the threatened destruction of the unfruitful planting. Contested because no fig tree appears, but the vineyard-judgment frame is coherent.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

registers.label: Spare
lines: Welcome, pilgrims on the way to the cross.
We are learning to follow Jesus.
The land is dry, and our souls are thirsty.
We thirst for the living God.
Come to the waters, all who have no money; come, buy and eat.
We come; let us worship the Lord who satisfies.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Can you feel the thirst — the dry and weary land where there is no water, the tongue that cleaves for want of a spring?
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
You who have no money, you who have spent it all on what does not satisfy, come to the waters and drink.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
The gardener kneels at the barren tree, loosens the soil, and pleads for one more year.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
So seek the Lord while he may be found; come to the table he has spread.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Our souls thirst in a dry and weary land.
Turn us, O God, and we will return.
Come to the waters, all who are thirsty; come and drink.
Turn us, O God, and we will return.
The tree is given one more year to bear; seek the Lord while he is near.
Turn us, O God, and we will return. Amen.
